title: Redraw the district lines and 40% of the votes can win 60% of the seats
body: Each US state draws its own House districts, normally once a decade after the census. Whoever holds the pen can **pack** the other side’s voters into a few districts they win by huge margins and **crack** the rest across districts they narrowly lose, so the same votes can produce very different seat counts. The trick is named after Elbridge Gerry, the Massachusetts governor who in 1812 signed a map with a state senate district likened to a salamander. For the 3 November 2026 midterms, [10 states have adopted new congressional maps](https://www.nbcnewyork.com/news/politics/house-redistricting-gop-democrats-2026-midterm-elections/6508364/) in the middle of the decade: eight whose maps NBC News expects could help Republicans by up to 16 seats, and California and Utah, where new maps could help Democrats by up to 6.

slides.question: 60% of 50 voters are purple, 40% orange. With five districts of ten voters, how many seats can a map hand orange at most?
slides.explanation: 3. Orange needs 6 of 10 voters to win a district outright, and its 20 voters can fill only three such districts. Purple is left with two lopsided wins.

slides.alt: Animation on drafting paper: a grid of 30 purple and 20 orange voters is cut into five districts three ways, giving purple 5 seats to 0, then 3 to 2, then orange 3 to 2. A salamander recalls the 1812 gerrymander, and tiles show the ten states with new maps for 2026.

slides.prompt: Paint five districts of ten joined-up voters. Can you make orange, with 40% of the voters, win 3 of the 5 seats?
slides.takeaway: Pack purple into two districts and let orange win the other three 6 to 4: 40% of the votes, 60% of the seats. Any map you draw is a choice about who wins.

slides.heading: Packing and cracking
slides.text: **Packing** squeezes the other side’s voters into a few districts, where most of their votes are wasted on huge wins. **Cracking** spreads them thinly across many districts, where they narrowly lose everywhere. Most gerrymanders use both.

slides.heading: Who draws the lines
slides.text: In many states the legislature draws the maps, so the party in power does. Some states hand the job to independent commissions, and courts can throw out maps that break state or federal law: before 2026 a Utah judge rejected a map for breaking the state’s anti-gerrymandering rules.

slides.question: What does “cracking” mean in redistricting?
options: Spreading a group’s voters thinly across districts
Packing a group into one district
slides.explanation: Cracking spreads a group’s voters across many districts so they fall short everywhere. Packing does the opposite: it concentrates them where their extra votes are wasted.
